It's when people stop caring about property value that they tend to produce the most interesting and authentic living environments.

Artists have always sought-out the urban detritus--the abandoned/neglected places in the habitat--in search of low cost live/work space. Places where they can express their creativity in the habitat without the hassles of bureaucrats and busybodies telling them what they can and can't do. This goes back as long as there have been professional artists of one kind or another. And they tend to be tribal--influenced by and drawn to each other--creating communities. They apply novel, quirky, 'adaptive reuse' to the local architecture to make it suit their needs and imaginations. The 'lofting' movement of the '70s was started by artists who moved into the abandoned industrial buildings of the early 20th century and turned them into unique live/work homes. Now developers purpose-build loft buildings.

The rich, who are artists' primary customers, desire nothing so much as to share the bohemian lifestyle of the artists they admire. And so when artists have established their communities in these neglected places the rich soon follow to try and glom-onto the quirky local aesthetic and community atmosphere those artists have created. But rich folk have a tendency to ruin everything they touch. Just their presence alone drives real estate values up, putting them in competition for space with the artists that are the very reason why they were drawn there. They want that bohemian lifestyle, but on their terms, without compromises on their comforts and conveniences. And so the character of the community is changed. Soon the community is being dominated by the presence of these rich people, there are bureaucrats and busybodies telling people what can and can't be done, corporate developers are mass-producing their bastardized versions of the local aesthetic, and the real estate value has been pushed beyond the reach of the artists who originally created the community. And so they are forced to move on, to other urban detritus, and the process starts all over again.

In this century artists have been joined by other types of creatives lumped together under the term 'creative class'. Music, fine crafts, specialty foods, independent publishing, coding and web development, independent tech development, political and environmental activists, and so-called 'social entrepreneurs'. (people who pursue business startups with lofty social missions) Many are so-called trust-fund babies who have woken up to their pathetic parasitic existence and now want to actually cultivate their creativity and have positive impact on the world --though they still tend to crave their comforts and suffer from class biases/myopia. They seek out the same kinds of urban detritus to repurpose, create the same kinds of quirky novel habitats that draw the attention of their wealthy followers, and have the same effect on real estate as the artists before them, now at a sometimes faster pace as so many of them are well-heeled to begin with. They, ironically, often gripe to each other about the gentrification they themselves are inducing, now that real estate investors dog them in order to exploit their influence. In the past decade a new kind of development has become common; live/work loft developments. Purpose-built housing developments designed to combine residential and work spaces in order to appeal to these creatives.

So there's nothing really new in all this. This process has been going on in cities for a long time. The reason it isn't as common in the small rural towns is that there is no nearby market for those creatives' products in those towns. And venture capitalists have this tendency to only invest in things that are within casual pestering distance of where they live. That's why there's a Silicon Valley. But that is changing a bit in recent times as mobile communications is making location less critical, creating a new Digital Nomad phenomenon in combination with the Startup Culture that now sees startup hot-spots popping up in remote parts of the world.
